nameStory: The name "catsfoot" comes from the fuzzy, soft flower heads that feel remarkably like the underside of a cat's paw pad when you gently touch them. This little plant also goes by "pussytoes" for the same reason - those papery, velvety flower clusters are irresistibly pet-able and remind everyone of feline feet.
description: Catsfoot is a low-growing perennial wildflower that forms small mats or patches close to the ground. The plant rarely grows taller than 6 inches and spreads by underground runners called stolons. Its most distinctive feature is clusters of small, papery white or pinkish flower heads that feel soft and fuzzy to the touch. The leaves are small, spoon-shaped, and covered in fine silvery hairs that give them a woolly appearance.

idTips.label: Texture

habitat: In New England, catsfoot is extremely rare and typically found in cool, mountainous areas with well-drained, sandy or rocky soils. It prefers open, sunny spots like alpine meadows, rocky slopes, or disturbed areas at higher elevations. Given its northern and mountainous preferences, any New England sighting would likely be in the White Mountains of New Hampshire or similar high-elevation locations.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge early, covered in distinctive silvery hairs that make the plant look woolly and soft.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time when the characteristic soft, papery flower clusters appear and are most easily identified by touch.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may persist into early fall, though they become more papery and less vibrant in color.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to ground level, leaving only underground runners to survive the cold.

funFact: Despite being called "catsfoot," this plant is actually more closely related to daisies and sunflowers than to anything feline - it's the incredibly realistic cat-paw-like texture of the flowers that earned it this purr-fect name!
confusionNotes: Catsfoot can be confused with its close relatives like Field Pussytoes or Small Pussytoes, but catsfoot typically has more silvery-white foliage and tends to grow in cooler, more mountainous locations. Remember: if it feels exactly like a cat's paw and you're up high in the mountains, you've likely found the rare catsfoot.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name "dioica" means "two houses," referring to the fact that male and female flowers grow on separate plants. This is unusual in the plant world and means you need both types of plants nearby for successful reproduction.
compareHints: Catsfoot differs from other New England pussytoes by its preference for cooler, mountainous habitats and its particularly silvery-white, woolly appearance. While Field Pussytoes and Small Pussytoes are more common in lower elevations and warmer sites, catsfoot seeks out the cool mountain air. The texture is similar across the genus, but catsfoot often has the most intensely fuzzy, cat-paw-like feel to its flower heads.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Small Pussytoes lives up to its name by being noticeably smaller than its relatives - its leaves are typically under 2 inches long compared to Field Pussytoes which can have 4-inch leaves.
Field pussytoes differs from small pussytoes by being taller and having more flower heads per cluster.

Among the pussytoes species in New England, plantain-leaved pussytoes is distinguished by its notably broader, more prominently veined leaves compared to field pussytoes or small pussytoes, which have much narrower, less obviously ribbed foliage.
Parlin's pussytoes is generally more robust and taller than Small Pussytoes, and has broader, more spoon-shaped leaves compared to the narrower leaves of Field Pussytoes.
